procedural_history.impugned_order: Reference by the President of India under Article 317(1) of the Constitution, asking the Supreme Court to consider whether a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission should be removed from office due to gross misbehavior.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: No High Court involvement mentioned in the provided text.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court issued notices and heard arguments from the Attorney-General of India and the Advocate-General of Punjab. The court is considering the procedure under Article 145 for regulating the practice and procedure of the Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the President must refer a case to a fact-finding body to ascertain if a prima facie case exists before making a reference to the Supreme Court under Article 317(1).

facts: A member of the Punjab Public Service Commission was accused of misbehaviour.
The President, under Article 317(1) of the Constitution, referred the matter to the Supreme Court to inquire whether the member should be removed.
The member's counsel argued that before making this reference, the President should have first used a separate fact-finding body to determine if there was a prima facie case.
law: Article 317(1) of the Constitution grants the President the power to make a reference to the Supreme Court for an inquiry into the alleged misbehaviour of a Public Service Commission member.
application: The Supreme Court examined the text of Article 317(1) and found no provision requiring the President to conduct a preliminary inquiry through another body before making a reference.
The Court stated that it was unjustified to read a "condition precedent" into the Article that was not explicitly there.
It held that the President's power to make a reference is not subject to the condition of first having the facts examined by some other authority.
The Court also noted that in this specific case, such a preliminary inquiry would amount to a "needless duplication of work and avoidable waste of public time and money."
The Court found that the material the President had was sufficient to justify his opinion that a prima facie case existed for an inquiry by the Supreme Court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the President is not required to refer a case to a preliminary fact-finding body before making a reference to the Court under Article 317(1). The President's power to make a reference is not subject to any such condition precedent.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court's inquiry in a reference under Article 317(1) is limited to determining if the alleged conduct amounts to misbehaviour, without examining the facts of the case itself.

law.fact: Article 317(1) of the Constitution provides that a member of a Public Service Commission can be removed by the President for misbehaviour only after the Supreme Court, on inquiry, reports that the member is guilty and ought to be removed.
law.reasoning: The Court interpreted the plain words of this article to mean that the Supreme Court itself must conduct the inquiry.

law.fact: Order XXXVIII, Rule 2 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1966, which regulates references under Article 317(1), states that "the Court may summon such witnesses as it considers necessary."
law.reasoning: The Court reasoned that this rule, allowing it to summon and hear evidence from witnesses, demonstrates that its function includes examining the facts of the case, not just reviewing findings made by another body.

application.fact: An argument was made that the Court's role should be limited to determining if facts, already found by another body, constitute misbehaviour warranting removal, and that the Court should not act as a trial court by examining the facts itself.
application.reasoning: The Supreme Court rejected this argument, stating it was in "direct opposition" to the plain language of Article 317(1). The Court clarified that the inquiry required by the article is not a limited review but an inquiry "into the facts themselves." The power to summon witnesses under its own rules further confirmed that the Court is required to undertake a fact-finding investigation.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that its inquiry is limited. It held that based on the plain words of Article 317(1) and its own procedural rules (Order XXXVIII, Rule 2), its constitutional duty is to conduct a full inquiry into the facts of the alleged misbehaviour itself, including summoning and hearing witnesses, before reporting its findings to the President.

issue.issue_text: Whether it is procedurally improper for the Supreme Court to decide questions of fact in an Article 317(1) reference, as this function should be performed by a lower court.

facts: The President of India made a reference to the Supreme Court under Article 317(1) of the Constitution to inquire into the alleged misbehaviour of a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission.
Counsel for the member argued that the Supreme Court should not act as a fact-finding body like a trial court.
The argument was that the Court's role should be limited to determining if facts, already established by a different body, constituted misbehaviour serious enough to warrant removal.

law.law_name: Article 317(1) of the Constitution of India
law.description: This article states that a member of a Public Service Commission can only be removed by the President for misbehaviour after the Supreme Court, on inquiry, has reported that the member ought to be removed.

law.law_name: Order XXXVIII, Rule 2 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1966
law.description: This rule provides that during an inquiry under Article 317(1), the Supreme Court may summon such witnesses as it considers necessary.

application.description: The Court first examined the plain text of Article 317(1). It concluded that the argument against fact-finding was in "direct opposition" to the article's wording. The Court held that the "inquiry" required by the article is not a limited review but an inquiry "into the facts themselves."

The Court then looked at its own procedural rules, specifically Order XXXVIII, Rule 2. It reasoned that the power to summon witnesses and record their evidence explicitly shows that the Court is empowered to perform a fact-finding function during these references.

The Court rejected the suggestion that the President must first use a preliminary fact-finding body. It found no such "condition precedent" in the text of Article 317(1) and refused to read a provision into the Constitution that was not there.

Finally, the Court dismissed the concern that it was unfair for the highest court to decide facts. It stated that as long as the "essential safeguards of a fair adjudication are observed," there is no grievance in the facts being found by the Supreme Court rather than a lower court.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that it is not procedurally improper for it to decide questions of fact in a reference under Article 317(1). The Court found that the plain language of the Constitution and the Court's own rules explicitly contemplate that it will conduct an inquiry into the facts, including summoning witnesses and recording evidence, to determine if a member is guilty of misbehaviour.

issue.issue_text: Whether the inquiry under Article 317(1) can be decided solely on the basis of affidavits without allowing for the cross-examination of witnesses.

facts: A procedural issue arose regarding whether the inquiry should be decided based only on the affidavits filed by the parties or if cross-examination of the witnesses should be permitted.
The person subject to the inquiry, Shri Saini, alleged that he had been falsely implicated in the incident.
law: Under Order XXXVIII, Rule 2 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1966, the Court has the power to summon witnesses and record their evidence during an inquiry under Article 317(1).
Cross-examination is recognized as the best method for testing the credibility of a witness.
application: The Court determined that due to the "nature and gravity of the matter," it would not be conducive to justice to rely solely on affidavits.
It reasoned that serious allegations and counter-allegations, such as the claim of being falsely implicated, cannot be properly adjudicated without testing the credibility of the witnesses.
The Court emphasized that the best way to assess a witness's credibility is to subject them to cross-examination.

The Court also considered the significant impact its findings would have on potential future trials (civil or criminal) and the public importance of the matter, which transcended the private interests of the parties involved.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the inquiry could be decided on affidavits alone. It held that given the gravity of the allegations and the need to assess witness credibility, the parties must be permitted to cross-examine the opposing witnesses who had filed affidavits.

appellant_arguments: On behalf of the Member, it was contended that before making the reference, the President ought to have referred the case to a fact-finding body to ascertain whether a prima facie case had been made out.
respondent_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the respondent's counter-argument, but by appearing in the proceedings and participating in the evidence-recording process, they implicitly argued that no such prior fact-finding was necessary and the Supreme Court's inquiry was the correct procedure.

appellant_arguments: The Member contended that the function of the Supreme Court is limited to determining whether the alleged conduct constitutes misbehaviour requiring removal, implying the court should not conduct a factual inquiry into whether the conduct actually occurred.
respondent_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the respondent's argument, but their position, accepted by the court, was that the Supreme Court's inquiry necessarily includes an examination of the facts to determine if the misbehaviour is established.

appellant_arguments: The Member expressed the grievance that the examination and assessment of facts should be made by a lower court, such as a Magistrate or a Munsif, and not by the Supreme Court acting as a court of first instance.
respondent_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the respondent's argument, but the position accepted by the court was that as long as a full and fair opportunity is given to both sides, there is no procedural impropriety or unfairness in the Supreme Court deciding the questions of fact.

appellant_arguments: The argument that was rejected by the court is that the inquiry could be decided summarily on the basis of affidavits alone.
respondent_arguments: The argument accepted by the court is that a fair adjudication of facts requires that witnesses who have filed affidavits must be made available for cross-examination to test their evidence.

statutes.principle: To establish the procedure for removing a Chairman or member of a Public Service Commission, which requires an inquiry and report by the Supreme Court on a reference from the President. It also serves to ensure the independence and protect the tenure of such members.
To establish the Supreme Court's power to make rules for regulating its own practice and procedure, subject to any law made by Parliament.
Cited as a procedural comparison for the removal of Supreme Court Judges, highlighting the protective nature of the tenure afforded to high-level dignitaries.
Cited as an example of a constitutional provision that provides similar procedural protection for the tenure of High Court Judges.
Cited as an example of a constitutional provision that provides similar procedural protection for the tenure of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India.
Relied on as the procedural rule governing the reference, into which other inherent powers of the court must be read to pass proper orders.
To affirm the Court's inherent power to act 'ex debito justitiae' (as a matter of right/justice) and pass proper orders, even if not explicitly incorporated in other specific rules.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The inherent power of the Supreme Court to make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice, as preserved under Order XLVII, Rule 6 of the Supreme Court Rules, must be read into other procedural orders, such as Order XXXVIII, even if not explicitly incorporated therein. Consequently, while the Court has the power to summon and examine witnesses, it is not required to record the evidence itself and may delegate that function to pass proper orders in the interest of justice.
obiter: If the essential safeguards of a fair adjudication are observed, no grievance can be made that the facts which establish a charge are found by the highest court and not by the lowest.

A finding of fact by the Supreme Court, after a full opportunity has been given to the parties, will determine the outcome of related prosecution or civil suits, and there is no unfair advantage to either side if the questions of fact are decided by the Supreme Court straightaway.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court's inquiry in a reference under Article 317(1) is a comprehensive, original fact-finding investigation to determine if allegations of misbehaviour against a Public Service Commission member are proven. This inquiry is not contingent on any prior fact-finding by another body before the President makes the reference, nor is it limited to merely opining on whether established facts constitute misbehaviour. As long as the essential safeguards of a fair adjudication are observed, giving both parties a full opportunity to prove and rebut facts as in a regular trial, it is procedurally proper for the Supreme Court itself to conduct this factual assessment.
legal_tests_applied: Interpretation based on the 'plain words' of Article 317(1) of the Constitution.
Adherence to 'the essential safeguards of a fair adjudication', which includes providing a 'full opportunity' to parties 'to prove and rebut the facts in issue as in a regular trial'.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the President must first refer the case to a fact-finding body was rejected because the power under Article 317(1) 'is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority.' The Court found 'no justification for reading into the Article a provision which is plainly not to be found in it'.

The contention that the Court's inquiry is limited to the nature of the misbehaviour, not the facts, was rejected as being 'in direct opposition to the plain words of article 317.(1).' The Court clarified that the inquiry 'is not into the limited question whether, on the basis of facts found by the President, the charge of misbehaviour is made out' but is 'into the facts themselves... so as to enable this Court to pronounce upon the question whether the allegations... were proved at all.'

The grievance that a lower court should decide questions of fact was dismissed because 'If a full opportunity is given to the parties to prove and rebut the facts in issue as in a regular trial, it is an idle complaint that the evidence has been examined and found upon by the Supreme Court and not by a court of first instance.'

The implied argument that the inquiry could be decided summarily on affidavits was rejected by the Court's insistence on a full and fair process, stating that if 'the essential safeguards of a fair adjudication are observed, no grievance can be made that the facts which establish the charge of misbehaviour are found by the highest Court of the land'.
why_respondent_won: The President's power to make a reference under Article 317(1) is not conditional on a prior inquiry, as no such condition precedent exists in the text of the Article.
The inquiry mandated by Article 317(1) is a comprehensive examination 'into the facts themselves' to determine if the allegations are proven, not a limited review of facts found by another body.

The procedure of the Supreme Court deciding facts is not improper as long as the process is fair. The Court held, 'There is, therefore, no unfair advantage to either side if the questions of fact are decided by this Court straightway. If the essential safeguards of a fair adjudication are observed, no grievance can be made...'

A full inquiry, akin to a regular trial with opportunities to prove and rebut evidence, is the correct procedure, which implicitly requires more than just affidavits and allows for processes like cross-examination to ensure a fair adjudication.
policy_considerations: Requiring a preliminary fact-finding inquiry before the President's reference 'would be needless duplication of work and avoidable waste of public time and money.'

The purpose of Article 317(1) is 'to ensure the independence of, members of the Public Service Commissions and to give them protection in the matter of their tenure' by having allegations examined on the merits by the Supreme Court.

There is no inherent unfairness in the Supreme Court deciding facts, as a finding can go either way: 'a contrary finding by this Court will equally seal the fate of those proceedings. There is, therefore, no unfair advantage to either side if the questions of fact are decided by this Court straightway.'
